passages.t: Pray for us; the Lord is faithful
passages.happening:
“Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may spread quickly and be held in honor, just as it was with you. And pray that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men; for not everyone holds to the faith” (verses 1-2).

“But the Lord is faithful, and He will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one. And we have confidence in the Lord that you are doing and will continue to do what we command. May the Lord direct your hearts into God’s love and Christ’s perseverance” (verses 3-5).
passages.hearers:
Paul asks a young, persecuted church to pray for him. The apostle needs their help. He asks for two things. First, that ‘the word of the Lord may spread quickly’. The word for ‘spread quickly’ means to run, and it was used of runners in a race. Paul pictures the message racing from town to town. Second, that he would be rescued from ‘wicked and evil men’. If Paul was in Corinth, he faced opposition there too (Acts 18:12-13).

‘Not everyone holds to the faith.’ Paul says it plainly. Not everyone will believe, and some will fight against it.

Then there is a play on words. Not everyone has faith, ‘But the Lord is faithful’. People may let you down. The Lord does not. He will ‘strengthen’ them, the same word used in 1 Thessalonians 3:2 for making something firm, and ‘guard’ them from ‘the evil one’.

The prayer in verse 5 is lovely. ‘Direct your hearts’ means to make the way straight and guide along it. Paul prays that their hearts will travel straight into God's love, and into ‘Christ's perseverance’. That may mean the endurance Christ gives, or the endurance Christ himself showed on the way to the cross. Either way, a waiting church looks to him for strength to keep going.
passages.ot:
The word running is a picture from the Psalms: “He sends forth His command to the earth; His word runs swiftly” (Psalm 147:15).

The prayer to be rescued from evil men is David's prayer: “Rescue me, O LORD, from evil men. Protect me from men of violence” (Psalm 140:1). And the promise of guarding is the psalmist's: “The LORD will guard you from all evil; He will preserve your soul” (Psalm 121:7).

And the faithfulness of God is the steady ground of the Old Testament: “He is the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just. A God of faithfulness without injustice” (Deuteronomy 32:4). “They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23).
passages.asks: Paul asked a young church to pray for him, and told them the Lord is faithful. Ask whom you could pray for whose work is hard right now. Ask where people have let you down, and whether you have let that shake your trust in the Lord. And ask where your heart needs a straight road into God's love.

passages.t: ‘If anyone is unwilling to work’: earn your bread, and do not tire of doing good
passages.happening:
“Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to keep away from any brother who leads an undisciplined life that is not in keeping with the tradition you received from us” (verse 6).

Paul points to his own example. “For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not undisciplined among you, nor did we eat anyone’s food without paying for it. Instead, in labor and toil, we worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to any of you. Not that we lack this right, but we wanted to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate” (verses 7-9).

“For even while we were with you, we gave you this command: ‘If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.’ Yet we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives and accomplishing nothing but being busybodies. We command and urge such people by our Lord Jesus Christ to begin working quietly to earn their own living. But as for you, brothers, do not grow weary in well-doing” (verses 10-13).
passages.hearers:
Paul had touched on this problem in his first letter, gently (1 Thessalonians 4:11-12; 5:14). Now it has grown, and he speaks firmly.

The problem was a group of people who were able to work and had stopped. They were living off the generosity of other believers, and filling their days with other people's business. Paul makes a play on words in verse 11 that English cannot quite keep: they were not busy at work, but busy at being busybodies.

Why had they stopped? Paul does not say. Some think the excitement about the Lord's coming in chapter 2 made ordinary work seem pointless. Others note that in Greek and Roman cities many poorer free men attached themselves to a rich patron, who supported them in return for loyalty and company in public. Perhaps some treated the church's generous members as new patrons. The two may have worked together.

The word ‘undisciplined’ means out of order, like a soldier who breaks ranks. It is not only about being lazy. It is about living outside the pattern the church had been taught.

Paul's answer is his own life. He had a right to be supported, as he argues at length in 1 Corinthians 9. But in Thessalonica he did not use it. He paid for his food and worked night and day, so that his life would be a pattern. In that world many of the upper classes looked down on work with the hands as fit for slaves. Paul did not.

Then the rule: ‘If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.’ And the words for the givers: ‘do not grow weary in well-doing’. Paul protects the church's generosity, so that it is not used up by those who could work, and so that it is still there for those who cannot.
passages.ot:
Work is part of the life God gave from the beginning. The law says, “Six days you shall labor and do all your work” (Exodus 20:9). Proverbs praises the one who works: “He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son” (Proverbs 10:5).

But the same Old Testament makes care for the poor a command. “For there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11). Farmers were to leave the edges of their fields for the poor and the foreigner to gather (Leviticus 19:9-10), and Ruth, a poor widow, gathered grain that way (Ruth 2:2-3). Proverbs says, “Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD” (Proverbs 19:17), and it warns that the poor can lose everything through injustice, not idleness: “without justice it is swept away” (Proverbs 13:23).

And God gives strength to those who do not tire of doing good: “He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak” (Isaiah 40:29).
passages.hard:
Does ‘If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat’ mean the church, or anyone, should refuse help to the poor?

No. The word is ‘unwilling’, not ‘unable’. Paul is speaking about particular people in that church who were able to work, refused, and lived off others while meddling in their affairs. The same letters tell the church to ‘help the weak’ (1 Thessalonians 5:14), and the early church took special care of widows, orphans and the sick.

So this verse is never a word against the poor, the sick, the disabled, people who cannot find work, people caring for others, or people who receive help. Using it that way goes against the letter it comes from, and against the whole Bible's care for the poor. As the site's wisdom topic on money says of a saying in Proverbs, it is a true word about how life usually goes, not a verdict on every poor person.

Christians differ on how far this verse reaches beyond the church, and on how a society should care for the poor. Some put the weight on charity, churches and neighbours, and are wary of looking to government for what neighbours are called to give. Others hold that just laws and public provision are also among the ways a society answers God's commands about the poor. The site's wisdom topic on justice and the poor sets out both, each as its holders would put it. These notes do not choose, and this verse is not a slogan for any side. On every view, believers are called to give and to act.

And notice where Paul ends: not with the idle, but with the givers. ‘Do not grow weary in well-doing.’
passages.asks: Paul asks the able to work and the generous not to grow tired of giving. Ask whether you are pulling your weight in the work in front of you. Ask whether you have used this verse to judge people whose lives you do not know. And ask whether you have grown weary of doing good, and where you could find strength to go on.

passages.t: Warn him as a brother; the Lord of peace be with you
passages.happening:
“Take note of anyone who does not obey the instructions we have given in this letter. Do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother” (verses 14-15).

“Now may the Lord of peace Himself give you peace at all times and in every way. The Lord be with all of you. This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. This is my mark in every letter; it is the way I write. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you” (verses 16-18).
passages.hearers:
The church met in homes and shared meals together. ‘Do not associate with him’ meant pulling back from that shared table for a time. In that world shame was a powerful force, and Paul uses it on purpose: ‘so that he may be ashamed’. The goal is that the person will see what he is doing and change.

But Paul at once sets a limit. ‘Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.’ The person is still family. The door is not shut. Discipline in this letter is meant to bring someone back, not to drive them out.

Then the closing prayer: ‘the Lord of peace Himself give you peace at all times and in every way’. A church that had been frightened and divided needed peace more than anything. Paul gives Jesus a title that belongs to God, ‘the Lord of peace’.

Letters were usually written down by a trained scribe while the author spoke, and the sender often added a closing line in his own hand to show the letter was genuine. Paul does that here. After the warning about a letter ‘seeming to be from us’ (2:2), his handwriting is the mark the church can trust.

Notice the last words: grace ‘with all of you’. Paul says ‘all’ three times in these closing verses. That includes the idle brother who is being warned.
passages.ot:
The law joins honest warning with love: “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him” (Leviticus 19:17). Proverbs says, “Better an open rebuke than love that is concealed. The wounds of a friend are faithful” (Proverbs 27:5-6).

And the closing prayer for peace echoes the old priestly blessing: “may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:26).
passages.hard:
Should churches still practise this kind of discipline, and how?

Churches have answered in different ways. Some can keep a person from Communion for a time, hoping to bring them back. Some practise church discipline carried out by elders, and some by the whole congregation. Others use little formal discipline and rely on pastoral care. These notes do not choose among the churches' practices. All can take Paul's limit: the person is ‘a brother’, not an enemy, and the aim is to bring him back.

This passage has also been badly misused, and that must be faced. Church discipline must never be used to silence someone who has been harmed, to protect someone who has done harm, or to punish someone for asking questions or telling the truth. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). A church meeting is never a substitute for that.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. Paul's goal was always restoration and comfort, never cruelty or contempt. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul tells the church to warn a wayward member as a brother, not to treat him as an enemy. Ask whether there is someone you have written off whom you should still treat as family. Ask whether you can hear a warning from a friend without treating them as an enemy. And ask where you need the Lord of peace to give you peace, at all times and in every way.
